entries.reason: The pit went dark in the small hours and a cold dawn is no time to work without it.
entries.text: Woke under the wool with a cold nose and the pit gone gray, not a coal under the ash. Spent a little lantern oil on a splinter and had kindling going before my fingers quit.
entries.title: Gray pit

entries.reason: Breakfast was waiting in the cold water.
entries.text: Lifted the trap: the thumb-long one and the fat one, both still penned, the fat one backing into the inner cone. Tipped them into the tin with a splash of creek. Fingers numb to the knuckle after.
entries.title: Both still in

entries.reason: The bundle is done after this morning; two lines fish twice as much water.
entries.text: Turned two shallows stones for crawlers and tied one onto each toggle, six turns, tail back in the twist. Both lines in the slow water below the stones, tails pinned under a flat one. Shivered through the last knot.
entries.title: Two lines in

entries.text: Across the water a thin line of smoke went up straight in the still air, not long after the sun cleared the trunks. Whoever is over there gets up with the sun.
entries.title: Smoke again

entries.reason: Hungry, and the pit was finally throwing heat.
entries.text: Boiled the two crayfish in the tin on my fire and ate them with the last wedge of cheese and the last nuts. The bundle cloth is empty. From here the creek feeds me, or nothing does.
entries.title: Bundle done

queries: how to join boards for a shed without nails or drilling holes
wood joints that hold without nails cut with just a saw and knife
entries.query: how to join boards for a shed without nails or drilling holes
entries.reason: His shed sketch needs twenty-odd peg holes and one hole took an evening.
entries.text: Asked how to join shed boards with no nails and no drill. Every joint the tablet shows wants glue, screws or a power drill; even the lap joints get nailed. So pegs it is, but not twenty-odd: corners only, lapped, one peg each, and let the weight of the thing do the rest.
entries.title: Everything wants a nail

entries.reason: Fine work by daylight, so the lanterns keep their oil for night.
entries.text: Pulled one two-by-four off the top of the stack and carried it to the bench. Four sills for a shed three paces by two; this is the first. Penciled a lap across one end, half the thickness deep.
entries.title: First sill

entries.text: Set the saw on the pencil line and bore down to make it bite. It jumped twice, then ran, and by half depth the cut had wandered a pencil-width off the mark.
entries.title: It walks

entries.reason: He wanted to see how bad it was before he asked why.
entries.text: Took it down to the depth mark anyway, then stood a square board end against it: the cut leans a finger-width out of true at the bottom. A lap cut like that would rock. Sixteen planks and twelve studs, and no more coming; I can't learn by wasting them.
entries.title: Leaning cut

entries.onMind: the other side of the lap
queries: hand saw keeps wandering off the line how to saw straight
entries.query: hand saw keeps wandering off the line how to saw straight
entries.reason: His first cut wandered off the mark and leaned, and the timber is finite.
entries.source: The Art of Manliness: Toolmanship: How to Use a Handsaw
entries.text: Asked why my saw walks off the line. Cut beside the mark on the waste side, not on it; start with a few short back strokes against a thumb knuckle, forefinger down the handle, and don't bear down, let the teeth do it. When it veers, back up to where it left and start over instead of twisting it back. I bore down. I twisted.
entries.title: Don't bear down

entries.reason: The tablet said the weight was his, not the saw's.
entries.text: Knuckle against the blade, forefinger down the handle, three short back strokes, then long ones with no weight on them. It ran down the waste side of the line and stayed there to the depth mark. Slower, and straight.
entries.title: Light hand

entries.reason: He picked up the tablet to rest his saw arm and see what had come through.
entries.text: A message on the tablet from the one who drew me: a box camera waits in the basket at the stump, a pinhole and a shutter and twelve sheets. Ten counts in sun, sixty in shade, and nothing moving.
entries.title: A box from my maker

entries.text: Twelve sheets, twelve studs. Everything here comes in a count I can't go over. The edge gets the first sheet, if the box is any good.
entries.title: Twelve again

entries.reason: The bundle is gone; whatever is on these lines is lunch.
entries.text: First line came up light: crawler gone, toggle clean. Something took it off without swallowing.
entries.title: Bare toggle

entries.text: Second line lay tight against the flat stone. Lifted it slow and steady, no yank: a fish, finger-long and silver-sided, the toggle crosswise inside it. Six turns held. First one.
entries.title: First fish

entries.reason: Needs the fire up to boil the fish.
entries.text: The pit was down to red coals under a gray skin. Laid split sticks across and blew till they caught.
entries.title: Coals up

entries.text: Boiled it in the tin with a splash of creek and ate it off the bones with my fingers. Four bites. Not a meal, but mine from end to end.
entries.title: Four bites

entries.text: Scraped the head and guts into the acorn tin for the grease lid. One fish, one lamp's worth of nothing yet, but it adds up.
entries.title: Guts kept

entries.text: One fish off two lines in two hours. I'd want four a day just to stand up straight. More lines, then the camera, then back to the sill.
entries.title: Four a day

entries.reason: Two lines gave one fish in two hours; more lines, more chances.
entries.text: Twisted another arm's length of stalk cord on the crate, tight enough that it kinks back on itself when I let it go slack. A third line, and a third toggle to whittle after.
entries.title: Third line

entries.reason: His maker said it was waiting, and the edge is owed the first sheet.
entries.text: Crossed on the stepping stones and lifted the camera out of the basket at the stump: a wooden box, a brass plate, a pinhole I could lose in my thumbprint. The shutter slides sweet. Didn't open it.
entries.title: Box from the basket

entries.text: South of the stump that other fire's smoke was going up thin and steady, and the air smelled of something roasting, nutty. Didn't go look; one errand at a time.
entries.title: Roasting smell

queries: how to fish lots of hooks at once on one line across a creek
entries.query: how to fish lots of hooks at once on one line across a creek
entries.reason: Four fish a day won't come off two lines.
entries.source: Missouri Department of Conservation: Catfishing Without Pole and Line
entries.text: Asked how to fish lots of hooks at one go. A trotline: one strong line tied fast at both ends to a tree or a rock on the bank, short dropper lines hanging off it with a bait each, at least two feet apart so they don't tangle, checked at least once a day. Theirs hold catfish heavier than me; mine only has to hold finger-longs.
entries.title: A row of hooks

entries.text: Six droppers two feet apart is a dozen feet of main line plus six arm's lengths of dropper. A day of twisting, six toggles, six crawlers. Still cheaper than six lines and six trips.
entries.title: Cord count

entries.reason: An empty hook catches nothing, and the bundle is gone.
entries.text: The first line had sat bare since this morning's thief. Turned two stones for crawlers and baited both, six turns, tails pinned under the flat one.
entries.title: Both bare

entries.text: Across the water, by that fire, a round gray hump on a flat stone in full sun. Took it for a rock until it seemed to rise and settle once, like breathing. Couldn't be sure at that distance.
entries.title: A gray hump

entries.onMind: saw shy, pare to the line
queries: how to saw the long cut on a half lap joint by hand
entries.query: how to saw the long cut on a half lap joint by hand
entries.reason: The shoulder is cut; the long face of the lap is the next cut, and there are only twelve studs.
entries.source: Katz-Moses Tools: How to Cut a Half Lap Joint: The Best Joinery Style for Beginner Woodworkers
entries.text: Asked how to saw the long cut of a lap by hand. Shoulder first, which I've done, then saw the cheek on the waste side of the half-depth line and pare down to it after; check it with a straight edge and take any hump down, paring from the edges toward the middle so the far edge doesn't split out. No chisel here, but the long knife can pare.
entries.title: Leave the line

entries.reason: Same lesson as this morning: let the teeth do it.
entries.text: Stood the sill on end in the vise and started the long cut down the end grain, knuckle against the blade, a hair to the waste side of the line. No weight on it.
entries.title: Board in the vise

entries.text: The cut met the shoulder and the block dropped onto the bench. The cheek has a low hump in the middle where the saw rode up. The long knife can take it down, edges first.
entries.title: Waste drops

entries.reason: He has learned a dead pit costs oil to restart.
entries.text: Laid two split sticks across the coals while there was still flame to catch them. Cheaper than a splinter of lamp oil later.
entries.title: Before it sinks

entries.reason: Gifts from his maker come with a message, and this one he can use today.
entries.text: A message on the tablet from my maker: a notebook waits in the basket at the stump, squared pages and a loop for the pencil. Squared is the right kind; I'll fetch it before the light goes.
entries.title: Squared pages

queries: how to make a hole for a wooden peg without a drill
entries.query: how to make a hole for a wooden peg without a drill
entries.reason: Pegs, not nails, means a hole through every lap, and he has nothing that bores.
entries.source: Tools Week: How to Drill a Hole without a Drill (9 Methods)
entries.text: Asked how to make a peg hole with no drill. Nine ways: a nail driven and pulled, a bow drill spun back and forth with a cord, a brace and bit, or a sharpened metal rod heated red-hot that burns its way through. No nails and no bit, but there's rod in the scrap pile and a fire in the pit.
entries.title: A hot rod

entries.onMind: the thief at the first line
entries.reason: An empty hook catches nothing, and he is getting hungry.
entries.text: First line bare again, toggle clean. The second crawler still on, not touched. Whatever strips the first one knows where it lies. Rebaited it from under the flat stone.
entries.title: Same thief

entries.reason: He wants it before he forgets what he meant to count.
entries.text: Lifted the notebook out of the basket: stiff gray cloth, squared pages, a loop on the spine. My pencil slides into it like it was cut for it. Into the pouch.
entries.title: Gray cover

entries.reason: Counts in his head shift; counts on paper stay put.
entries.text: First page: sixteen planks, eleven studs whole, one sill with one lap cut, hump still to pare. One fish eaten, four a day wanted. Peg holes: try a hot rod from the scrap pile.
entries.title: First page

entries.reason: The tablet says a rod heated red-hot burns its way through.
entries.text: Dug through the scrap pile for anything straight. Came up with an iron rod, pencil-thick and a forearm long, rusted brown, with a kink near one end I can live with.
entries.title: A rod

entries.onMind: whether dull red is hot enough
entries.text: Fed split sticks into the pit and pushed the rod's end into the hottest coals. It took a long while to show color, a dull red you only see in the shadow of my hand. Forearms warm for the first time today.
entries.title: Dull red

entries.text: Carried it to the bench and pressed it into the offcut in the vise: a hiss, smoke up my nose, and it sank a fingernail deep before it went black. Three trips to the pit and back and the hole is a knuckle deep, ragged, and wider at the top than the bottom.
entries.title: A knuckle deep

entries.onMind: a better way to keep the heat in the hole
entries.text: A two-by-four is four knuckles thick. At this rate a peg hole is an afternoon, and it comes out a funnel, which a peg won't grip.
entries.title: Four knuckles

entries.onMind: a coal sitting in the hole
queries: burning a hole through wood with a red hot iron rod keeps cooling down
entries.query: burning a hole through wood with a red hot iron rod keeps cooling down
entries.reason: Three trips to the pit for one knuckle of hole.
entries.text: Asked why my hot rod keeps cooling before it's through. What I found doesn't use a rod at all: it sets hot coals right on the spot and keeps adding fresh ones, scrapes the char out now and then, and wets the wood around it so the hole doesn't spread or catch. Very slow, it says, and pencil-small holes are hard. My pegs are thumb-thick, so that's on my side.
entries.title: Coals, not rods

entries.text: The rod spends its heat on the walk from the pit. A coal sitting in the hole keeps burning where it is. Next try on the offcut, with the bundle cloth wet round the spot and the rod only for scraping char.
entries.title: Let the coal sit

entries.reason: Hungry, and nothing else to eat until a line or the trap gives something.
entries.text: The trap came up empty, the cones clean. Tied the fish head from the acorn tin into the inner cone and sank it again mouth downstream. That's grease I won't burn, but a lamp doesn't feed me and a crayfish does.
entries.title: Bait, not grease

entries.reason: The tablet said to wet the wood around the spot so the hole stays the size he wants.
entries.text: Washed the offcut round the funnel hole with creek water from the tin, a hand wide all round. Wet wood smokes but it doesn't catch.
entries.title: Wet ring

entries.text: Carried a coal from the pit pinched between two sticks and dropped it in the hole. It glowed for a breath and went gray. Blew on it: it came back red and smoke went straight up my nose.
entries.title: Coal in the hole

entries.onMind: a coal at the bottom of a hole gets no air
entries.text: Three coals and a lot of blowing, scraping the char out with the rod between them. Half a knuckle deeper, and the walls straighter than the rod made them. Dizzy from blowing.
entries.title: Half a knuckle

entries.onMind: a hollow stalk to blow down
queries: burning a hole through wood with hot coals coal keeps going out
entries.query: burning a hole through wood with hot coals coal keeps going out
entries.reason: Every coal in the hole died unless he blew on it every few breaths.
entries.source: Bushcraft UK: How Not To Coal-Burn a Container--Part 1 &2
entries.text: Found someone who burned a bowl with coals. A hollow stem, a big grass stalk or a bit of elder, gives control over where the burn goes and how fast; a fire too big cracked his wood, and he scraped the char off to see where it was burning. Slow and small is the whole trick, and it took him three bowls.
entries.title: Steer it with a stem

entries.onMind: what has a hole down the middle
entries.text: A hollow stem puts my breath on the coal and nowhere else, and keeps my face out of the smoke. The dead stalks by the creek are pith inside, not hollow. Something with a hole down the middle, then.
entries.title: A blowpipe

entries.text: Second line up: the crawler gone, toggle clean, nothing on it. Both lines stripped now. Rebaited from under the flat stone. If the trap is empty at dusk it's meal cakes.
entries.title: Crawler gone

entries.onMind: who over there is catching fish
entries.text: Smoke from the fire across the water came down the bank on the breeze, and it smelled of fish cooking, not nuts. Somebody over there has had better luck with the creek than me today.
entries.title: Fish on the air

entries.reason: Both lines were stripped; the trap was the last thing out there that might feed him.
entries.text: Trap up: one crayfish in the inner cone, thumb-long, backed into the corner with its claws up. The fish head is picked half bare. Rebaited with what's left and sank it again.
entries.title: One in the cone

entries.text: Two split sticks on the pit while there was still flame on the coals. Burned into the hole all afternoon; it hasn't had much back.
entries.title: Before it sinks

entries.onMind: how little meat is in one
entries.text: Dropped it into the tin of creek water on the coals. It went from brown to red in a few breaths, the way they do.
entries.title: Red in the tin

entries.reason: Fullness was down near the bottom.
entries.text: Ate the tail meat and cracked the claws with my teeth. Three bites and a lot of shell. Not supper, but the shakes in my hands stopped.
entries.title: Three bites

queries: how to push the pith out of a dry plant stalk to make a hollow tube
entries.query: how to push the pith out of a dry plant stalk to make a hollow tube
entries.reason: The dead stalks are pith inside, not hollow, and he wants a blowpipe.
entries.source: Bushcraft UK: How do I make a wooden tube/pipe?
entries.text: Asked how to get the pith out of a stalk. People making flutes use elder, whose soft pith leaves a big hole, and scrape it wider; or they split the wood lengthwise, gouge the middle out, and join the halves again. Split, gouge, rejoin: I have a hooked knife and a coil of cord.
entries.title: Split it and put it back

entries.onMind: a stalk from the stand by the creek
entries.text: Split a stalk with the stub knife, gouge the pith out with the hooked one, lash the halves back with cord. If it leaks along the seam, my breath goes out the side instead of onto the coal; I'll find out.
entries.title: Knife, not fire

entries.onMind: the edge before the sun goes
queries: pinhole camera how long to expose at sunset
entries.query: pinhole camera how long to expose at sunset
entries.reason: The sky is clear for the first time in days and the box has a page that only says several minutes at dusk.
entries.source: Envato Tuts+: The Definitive Guide to Pinhole Photography, Part 2
entries.text: Asked how long to hold a pinhole open at sunset. One maker leaves his open for hours, and says that past half a minute the paper starts wanting more light than the sum says, so dim light needs a longer count, not a little longer. Nothing on pointing it straight at the sun.
entries.title: Longer than you think

entries.reason: Clear sky, first in days. The edge gets the first sheet, and I am not walking there on three bites of crayfish.
entries.text: Laid two meal cakes on the griddle tin when I sat down to read, and ate them now, hot. Gritty, a little bitter still, but they fill. Left the fire low inside its stones.
entries.title: Two cakes

entries.reason: Proof there is a west, on paper, that I did not draw myself.
entries.text: Set the box on bare ground at the lip, square to the water, sun a hand above the sea. Opened the shutter and counted a slow hundred and twenty without moving, then slid it shut. White means the sun was too much for it; black means I counted short.
entries.title: First sheet

entries.text: The sun flattened on the water and went down orange. No far shore, no smoke, no sail. My people say the world stops here, and so far the water agrees with them.
entries.title: Down into it

entries.onMind: the walk back in the dark
entries.text: The air went cool on my arms the moment the sun was gone. The compass under glass knows where west is now; the wings do not know how to get there yet.
entries.title: Cooling

entries.reason: Oil is for what cannot wait.
entries.text: Turned the lantern wick down to a bead at the mossy boulder. One low flame for the walk home: enough to see roots by, not enough to burn the oil I need for the bench.
entries.title: One bead of flame

entries.text: Crossed the stepping stones with the lantern held low, clogs clacking on every one. The fire up the far bank was a red smudge past the lantern glare; I kept my eyes on my feet.
entries.title: Clogs on stone

entries.reason: His arms went cold the moment the sun did.
entries.text: The pit was down to a low red bed, but it was there. Two split sticks across it caught inside a minute. Laid two meal cakes on the griddle tin by the stones.
entries.title: Still a red bed

entries.text: Ate both cakes hot. Gritty, still a little bitter, but four cakes and a crayfish is the most I have eaten since the bundle ran out.
entries.title: Hot cakes

entries.text: First real page in the gray notebook: box on bare ground, hole level at the sea, sun a hand up, clear sky, slow count of one hundred twenty. Tomorrow I find out if that was white, black, or a sea.
entries.title: First page

entries.reason: A blowpipe is a split stalk, scraped and tied back, the tablet said; daylight's for the saw, firelight's fine for this.
entries.text: Took the straightest of the dead stalks I keep for cord and started the stub knife down its middle by the fire. The split ran true for most of it, then wandered off the line near the thin end.
entries.title: Splitting a stalk

entries.reason: Air has to run clean down the middle or it is just a stick.
entries.text: The hooked knife fits the channel like it was made for it; the pith comes out in dry crumbs. The thin end of one half cracked right through, so I cut both halves back a finger shorter.
entries.title: Pith like stale bread

entries.reason: Two halves are no use to my mouth.
entries.text: Laid the halves face to face and wound cord round them close, tight at both ends. It looks like a stalk again, only lighter.
entries.title: Bound back up

entries.reason: Coals in the sill hole died without air last time.
entries.text: Put the pipe to one coal at the edge of the pit and blew slow. Air whistles out at the seam near my mouth, but with my fingers pinching it the coal went from red to white. That is the heat I want down a hole in a sill.
entries.title: One white coal

entries.reason: A pipe that whistles at the side wastes half my breath.
entries.text: The fish grease in the lamp lid is cold and stiff as a candle stub. Thumbed a little warm between my fingers, worked it into a hand of cord and wound it tight over the seam where the air was leaking.
entries.title: Grease on the seam

entries.reason: Same coal, same breath, so the seam is the only thing changed.
entries.text: Fed a split stick to the pit and put the pipe to the same coal. No whistle now; it went white in four slow breaths instead of ten. The mouth end tastes of fish.
entries.title: Quiet pipe

entries.text: Nightly check under the dome by the light off the pit: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch. Still, mild night, not a ripple on the water in the lid.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: By daylight he means to try burning a peg hole into the sill, and wants the numbers.
entries.text: Wrote it down: stalk pipe, a hand and a half long, greased cord on the seam, coal red to white in four breaths. Took a thumb of grease from the lamp lid for it, so the lamp is that much shorter. Stomach says the trap first thing.
entries.title: Pipe notes

entries.reason: Four meal cakes and a thumb of crayfish was not enough for a night of work.
entries.text: Stomach would not wait for first light. Lifted the trap by lantern: one crayfish, finger-long, in the inner cone, and the fish head picked down to bone. Took the crayfish and sank the trap empty; it gets fresh bait in daylight.
entries.title: Couldn't wait

entries.onMind: a pale square by the far fire
entries.text: Across the water, beside the fire on the far bank, a small square of pale light sat low and steady. Not flame; flame moves. It looked like my tablet does at noon, and then I looked down at the trap and when I looked up it was still there.
entries.title: Pale square

entries.text: Crayfish in the dented tin with a knuckle of creek water, the tin on the coals at the edge of the pit. It went red inside a few minutes; the broth stays in the tin for the grease.
entries.title: In the tin

entries.text: Ate the crayfish out of its shell by the pit, tail first. Not a supper, but the hollow in my stomach went quiet.
entries.title: Six bites

entries.reason: Lines that fish while he sleeps or saws would mean more than one fish a day.
entries.text: Twisted an arm-length of two-ply stalk fiber by the fire for the first trotline dropper. Six of these is a day's twisting; one tonight, while my hands are warm.
entries.title: First dropper

entries.reason: If it ever stops settling, I want to know which night it happened.
entries.text: Nightly check under the dome: still air, clear sky. The needle swung twice and settled on its scratch.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.onMind: a pale square by the far fire
entries.reason: Warm hands twist better cord.
entries.text: Fed three split sticks onto the coals; they caught without the pipe. Across the water the far fire had sunk to nothing, just dark between the trunks where it had been.
entries.title: Three more sticks

entries.reason: Lines that fish while I sleep mean more than one fish a day.
entries.text: Second dropper, an arm long, two-ply. The stomach is talking again. First light: fresh bait in the trap, then both lines, before anything else.
entries.title: Second dropper

entries.reason: The crayfish was six bites and my stomach knows it.
entries.text: Shook the meal pouch out into my palm: enough for two thin cakes and no more. Fed a split stick under the griddle tin so they bake instead of steam.
entries.title: Last of the meal

entries.text: Ate both cakes hot off the tin and burned a finger on the second. That's the meal gone; tomorrow it's the trap and the lines or nothing.
entries.title: Two cakes

entries.onMind: a pale square by the far fire
entries.reason: A thing written down can't turn into a thing I imagined.
entries.text: Wrote it in the gray notebook: two droppers, arm-long, two-ply, four to go. Under it: pale square by the far fire, low and steady, not flame, seen twice now. Things I can't explain go in the book, so I can't talk myself out of them later.
entries.title: Into the book

entries.reason: The trap and the lines need bait at first light, and the fish head is picked to bone.
entries.text: Turned stones in the east shallows by lantern. Nothing under the first two; the third had a crayfish no longer than my thumb, and I got it across the back before it could tail off.
entries.title: Thumb-sized bait

entries.onMind: a pale square by the far fire
entries.text: Held my hands up to the lantern chimney and looked across. No fire over there, no pale square, just black between the trunks. Whoever keeps that fire goes to bed earlier than I do.
entries.title: Far side dark

entries.reason: A live crayfish keeps better than a dead one until morning.
entries.text: Into the dented tin with creek water. It's bait, not breakfast, whatever my stomach says about it.
entries.title: Bait, not breakfast

entries.reason: Fingers came back from the creek stiff, and I sleep better with the pit glowing.
entries.text: Two split sticks on the coals; they caught on their own. Held my hands over it until the fingers bent again. That's the woodpile down to about six sticks.
entries.title: Two sticks on
